questions.questionText: What is the formula for price elasticity of demand (E_d) using the midpoint method?
questions.explanation: The midpoint formula divides the change in quantity and price by their averages, eliminating base‑dependency.

questions.questionText: If the price of a good rises from $4 to $5, what is the percentage change in price using the initial‑value method?
In the textbook example (price $10 → $14, quantity 100 → 60), what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Using the midpoint method gives E_d = -0.50/0.333 = -1.5; absolute value = 1.5.
|E_d| greater than 1 indicates quantity changes proportionally more than price, i.e., elastic demand.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best describes the Total Revenue Test?
options: Raise price when demand is elastic, lower price when inelastic
Raise price when demand is inelastic, lower price when elastic
questions.correctAnswer: Raise price when demand is inelastic, lower price when elastic
questions.explanation: If demand is inelastic, price increase raises total revenue; if elastic, price decrease raises revenue.

questions.questionText: Why do economists prefer percentage changes over simple slopes when measuring elasticity?
options: Percentages remove unit dependence, allowing comparison across goods
questions.correctAnswer: Percentages remove unit dependence, allowing comparison across goods
questions.explanation: Using percentages makes elasticity unit‑free, unlike slopes which vary with measurement units.

questions.questionText: If a good has a price elasticity of demand of |E_d| = 0.4, what happens to total revenue when price is increased?
options: Cannot be determined without quantity data
questions.explanation: |E_d| < 1 indicates inelastic demand; price increase outweighs quantity loss, raising revenue.

questions.questionText: Which of the following goods is most likely to have elastic demand?
options: A specific brand of soda with many substitutes
questions.correctAnswer: A specific brand of soda with many substitutes
questions.explanation: Goods with many close substitutes tend to be price‑sensitive, i.e., elastic.

The gain in producer surplus from a tax
The loss of total surplus that results from mutually beneficial trades not occurring
The total revenue lost by a firm when demand is elastic
questions.correctAnswer: The loss of total surplus that results from mutually beneficial trades not occurring
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss represents the welfare loss from prevented trades, shown as a triangle between supply and demand.

questions.questionText: How does the direction of price change affect simple percentage calculations?
options: It does not affect the percentage; both directions give the same result
An increase from $4 to $5 is 25% while a decrease from $5 to $4 is 20%
An increase always yields a larger percentage than a decrease of the same absolute amount
It only matters for elastic goods
questions.correctAnswer: An increase from $4 to $5 is 25% while a decrease from $5 to $4 is 20%
questions.explanation: Using the initial value creates a base‑dependency; the two directions give different percentages.
